extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and agents drafting or prosecuting biotech, chemical, and pharmaceutical patent applications (life sciences patent attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and construing patent claims in biotech/chemical/pharmaceutical applications, focusing on claim construction standards, Markush group drafting, and avoiding dependent-claim invalidation pitfalls. Emphasizes interaction of specification language, claim phraseology, MPEP guidance, and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of differing claim construction standards (USPTO examination vs. PTAB/courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO examination standard is the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim; post-grant proceedings before the PTAB and federal courts use the ordinary and customary meaning (the 'Phillips' standard). Both standards are viewed in the context of the person of skill in the art (POSITA) at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know which forum will apply which standard (BRI during examination, Phillips for PTAB/courts since Nov. 13, 2018). Strategically, drafting should account for both because both rely on POSITA and the specification; MPEP 2111 constrains BRI to be consistent with ordinary meaning and the specification. See Cuozzo, Phillips, and Federal Register notice changing PTAB standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting claim-term definitions in the specification (be your own lexicographer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider providing detailed definitions of claim terms in the specification; practitioners may act as their own lexicographers to define terms for claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a tradeoff: specifying definitions can lead courts to adopt narrower constructions than plain meaning, but current trends often favor detailed definitions. When defining terms, consider whether definitions differ from plain and ordinary meaning and whether to include a fallback definition that preserves broader plain-meaning coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the Person of Skill in the Art (POSITA) when construing and drafting claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Both BRI and Phillips standards interpret claims in the context of the POSITA at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame claim language and specification examples with the knowledge level and expectations of POSITA in mind; use specification disclosure to clarify ambiguous terms for that hypothetical skilled worker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush group membership requirement (recognized class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of a Markush group ordinarily must belong to a recognized physical or chemical class or to an art-recognized class (MPEP 803.02; Ex parte Markush).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting Markush groups, ensure listed members form an art-recognized class (chemical/physical grouping) to avoid challenges to claim correctness or interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's duty to examine all members of a Markush group when manageable
rubrics_metrics.description: If the members of a Markush group are sufficiently few in number or so closely related that a search and examination of the entire claim can be made without serious burden, the Examiner must examine all members on the merits and should not require provisional election of a single species (MPEP 803.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft Markush groups with awareness that closely related or limited lists will be fully examined; consider number and relationship of species to avoid unnecessary restriction or election issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language determines Markush openness/closedness ('consisting of' presumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of 'consisting of' creates a very strong presumption that a Markush group is closed (excludes unrecited elements); 'comprising' and certain phrases (e.g., 'at least one') can support an open interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume 'consisting of' will be construed as closed unless the specification or prosecution history unmistakably manifests otherwise (Shire). Use claim language carefully to secure desired openness or closedness; case examples: Abbott (presumed exclusion of mixtures), Shire (closed), Amgen (open due to 'at least one').

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification can alter interpretation of Markush groups (include blends if specification supports)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification that repeatedly and consistently references blends or teaches mixing member compounds can lead courts to construe a Markush group as including blends (Multilayer v. Berry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want Markush groups to cover mixtures/blends, explicitly describe blending and examples in the specification and use consistent language throughout prosecution to support that construction on litigation or enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice points for Markush drafting (include desired compounds; align dependent claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take care to include all desired compounds in a Markush group and ensure any compound recited in a dependent claim also appears in the independent claim's Markush group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omitting a compound from the independent claim's Markush list can render dependent claims improper or invalid. Use claim drafting checklists to confirm that dependent claim species are encompassed by their base claim's Markush group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claim proper form under 35 U.S.C. §112(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim in dependent form must contain a reference to a previous claim and 'specify a further limitation' of the claimed subject matter; it is construed to incorporate all limitations of the claim to which it refers (35 U.S.C. §112(d); MPEP 608.01(N)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure dependent claims truly further limit the base claim and do not introduce subject matter that the base claim did not permit (e.g., salts when the base claim was not open to salts). Failure to further limit can be an independent ground for invalidation (see Multilayer; Pfizer v. Ranbaxy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid improper dependent claims that introduce unrecited categories (examples: salts, homopolymers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims that add elements or categories not open in the base claim risk invalidation (e.g., dependent claim reciting 'low density polyethylene homopolymers' when the Markush group did not include that species).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check dependent claim limitations against the language and scope of the base claim; if the base claim is closed to certain categories, do not attempt to add them in a dependent claim without ensuring the base claim permits them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use MPEP and controlling case law to guide drafting choices
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP sections (e.g., 2111, 803.02, 608.01(N)) and Federal Circuit/Supreme Court cases (Phillips, Cuozzo, Multilayer, Abbott, Shire, Amgen, Pfizer, etc.) provide binding or persuasive guidance on claim construction, Markush interpretation, and dependent-claim form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult and cite relevant MPEP sections and case law when drafting/specifying claim language. Use prosecution history and specification drafting to support desired claim interpretations in view of precedent.
